title: Work in Progress
text: My book manuscript, A Working Democracy: Progressivism and the Politics of Work, is under review. It’s a study of Progressive Era intellectuals in the United States, how they thought about work, and what they thought it meant for democracy. One contribution the book makes is a new interpretation of Progressivism as an ideology that centers work, an ideology that tried to make space for cross-class solidarity. Along the way, it makes an argument for including W.E.B. Du Bois among the Progressives, alongside Jane Addams, John Dewey, and Charlotte Perkins Gilman. And it shows how figures like Herbert Croly of The New Republic magazine helped to synthesize and popularize their ideas in the period. I conclude by suggesting that there are aspects of the Progressives’ ideology of work that are worth keeping alive today, most of which are rooted in the Progressive intellectuals’ understanding of themselves as workers.

title: Work in Progress
section: Cold War social science in the United States
text:
Cold War social science in the United States
I’m also at work on an as-yet-unnamed project on the surprising interdisciplinary exchanges in U.S. social science during the Cold War. These exchanges gave rise to what we now consider mainstream American political science, and gave birth to a new field that was at the time called (by some of its progenitors) “policy sciences,” and which we now know as the discipline of “public policy.” I have presented work from this project at conferences of the Northeast Political Science Association, the Association for Political Theory, and the Social Science History Association. It’s based in archival sources, and is therefore even more slow-moving than my usual snail’s pace. With support from the American Philosophical Society and the Office of the Dean of Faculty, I am on leave during the 2026–27 academic year so that I can get this project off the ground. If you wish to follow the journey, then you can read my public notebook.

title: Enter Thomas Szasz
text:
In addition to Eric Berne, the current psychiatry project also considers Thomas Szasz, an important figure in the related anti-psychiatry and deinstitutionalization movements. The paper I’m currently working on as I write this update attempts to work out their relationship to one another and their relative importance to some of the intellectual currents of the time, notably the interdisciplinary formation we know as “game theory.” I’m writing this down to help clarify for myself what got me hooked on these two unusual figures.
I noticed the connection between them when I was seriously reading Games People Play. As I mentioned before, the book is dated and problematic in all kinds of ways. Nevertheless, I found it compelling as an intellectual document. One of the reasons that I found it so interesting is because my most important work at the time was a civic project that involved facilitating weekly group therapy with youth in jail who were facing adult charges. One of my co-facilitators was an older psychiatric social worker whose day job was in a state mental hospital. I’ve written about this elsewhere, if anyone is curious. It was a weird chapter of life. Knowing a little bit about Berne’s “transactional analysis” gave me at least one way of understanding the work we were doing, however dated his concepts.
But apart from its use in this specific and unusual collaboration, I have to admit that I found some of the “game analysis” verified in daily experience. My professional life kept showing me examples of Berne’s “Why Don’t You — Yes But” (YDYB) game. It had a bit of Myers-Briggs or Enneagram to it, the same parlor-game kind of appeal. Berne, however, didn’t see it as a parlor-game. When I looked at his footnotes, it was clear he saw it as a science. And it was clear that he saw it as a species of “game theory.” I’ve seen some confirmatory evidence in the Grove Press archives that suggest it wasn’t just Berne who saw it that way. I’m hoping to work it into this paper.
Berne’s collection of interlocutors for “game analysis” was an interesting collection of people, listed in the footnotes for his theoretical chapter: Stephen Potter’s book on Gamesmanship (a book I always thought of as a piece of popular humor writing), George Herbert Mead (a serious philosopher), and Thomas Szasz (a name that was altogether new to me). Berne also mentioned The San Francisco Social Psychiatry Seminar, which remains an intriguing institution to me. The Szasz citation was the most provocative. His book was called The Myth of Mental Illness, which seemed like an echo of my graduate-school reading of Foucault. Only I noticed that Szasz’s book appeared in 1961, the same year Foucault published Folie et déraison, a tantalizing coincidence.
But what made Szasz interesting for me, at the time, was how much he was involved in the relationship between psychiatry and the courts. Learning as much as I could about Szasz during the same months that I was spending one evening per week in jail alongside a psychiatric social worker made me aware of the relationship between mental health systems and the application of the law. It made Szasz more sympathetic to me, for better or for worse. It certainly helped me see the scope of the problem he was writing about, and its stakes.

title: Joel Winkelman
text:
I teach government and public policy at Hamilton College.
I’m from Oklahoma. I went to Hendrix College and did my PhD at UNC-Chapel Hill.
I’ve always got a new hobby going. The two that stuck are record collecting and rock climbing. I also tinker with computers more than I probably should.

title: Just another day at the office
text:
I want to write a little bit about the genesis of this project, mostly so that I don’t forget. It may also be useful to some reader to peek behind the curtain of how professors at liberal arts colleges work.
Part of where this project came from was a random blog post that I was reading about Murray Edelman, whose concept of “symbolic reassurance” is one of the most powerful and under-examined concepts in the discipline. I find that it’s even more powerful when considered in his own historical context. I’m liable to get bogged down if I write any more about Edelman, so I’ll try to get to the point. It’s going to take a second.
At the time, I was working in an administrative role at the college and didn’t have time to dedicate to serious scholarship. My curiosity was rather untethered and I indulged it in spare moments between trying to establish a program in “public philosophy” and implementation of an expanded, branded “experiential learning” initiative.
So, when I had time to read a blog post on Murray Edelman, I found stray references to an unknown-to-me author named Eric Berne and his book Games People Play. The post didn’t provide a satisfactory explanation of the connection between Berne and Edelman. And so the reference was like a fly to a brook trout: a hook in a swiftly moving stream.
Over the next few months, I put the pieces together of who Berne was: a Canadian who had trained in psychoanalysis and settled in Northern California. It didn’t take much: he’s reasonably well-documented online. He was mostly in private practice, not institutional. But he was well-known in his field as the founder of a therapeutic methodology called “transactional analysis.” Games People Play was a mature expression of this methodology. The book itself, I would learn, is a strange text: part textbook for therapists, part self-help, and partly a book for the general reader. It seemed self-conscious and like it was attempting humor, though most of what he seems to try and pass off as humor are bald-faced misogyny and homophobia. In that regard, parts of it are hard to get through.
In writing my paper on John Dewey I had come across the vocational guidance literature, so I had a basic mental model of how to understand Games People Play, but not one large enough to shake my curiosity off of it.
That’s where the project got its start: a random blog post on an afternoon between administrative tasks.
But I forgot to mention one thing: Games People Play wasn’t some obscure text from the 1960s. It had been a smash for its publisher. It was well-known enough that in 1968 Joe South released a song called “Games People Play,” which won the Grammy for Song of the Year. I’m pretty certain, though I haven’t been able to find the documentary connection that I would need to make the claim in academic writing, that South’s song is inspired by the book and its popularity. The Grove Press archives may have just what I’m after; a publisher like Grove would want their piece of the pie.
It has been recorded by something like two hundred artists since. King Curtis’s instrumental version (Duane Allman on guitar) won a Grammy of its own. Dolly Parton did a version. My favorite is Lee Dorsey’s, on Yes We Can (1970), produced by the inimitable Allen Toussaint.
As unsexy as that sounds, it’s how the project got started. Sometimes the life of the mind is just another day at the office.

title: Teaching
text: I’ve taught a range of courses over my career at Hamilton. The three I keep coming back to are American Political Process, Introduction to Public Policy, and a seminar on Capitalism, Democracy, and the Workplace.
